mainTopic: Coins in bought produce, the garment as the model for announcing lost items, why the Torah names each item, the פרוטה minimum, and whether סימנים are from the Torah.
overview: This עמוד opens by finishing a rule from the previous עמוד. Someone who finds coins in produce he bought may keep them only if he bought from a merchant, not from a private owner. רב נחמן questions a ברייתא that says this, and it is kept by reading it as a case where the owner's כנעני slaves did the threshing. A new משנה then teaches that the Torah singled out the שמלה (garment) to show that any lost item with סימנים and with owners who would claim it must be announced. רבא asks why the Torah lists an ox, a donkey, a sheep and a garment. He explains the donkey (signs on its saddle are enough) but admits that the word שה has no explanation. Next, a ברייתא teaches that an item worth less than a שוה פרוטה need not be returned. The תנא קמא and רבי יהודה learn this from different words in the פסוק. אביי says they differ only about the source. רבא finds a practical difference: an item whose value went up, down and up again. Finally the גמרא asks whether returning items based on סימנים is from the Torah or from the Rabbis, and what difference that makes. The answer continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: Merchant versus private owner
steps.stepSummary: The ruling that the buyer keeps found coins applies only when he bought from a merchant. If he bought from a private owner, he must return them.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies to someone who bought from a merchant. But someone who bought from a private owner must return the coins.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the end of a statement that began on the previous עמוד. It limits the rule that a buyer who finds coins in produce may keep them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A תגר buys his stock from many sellers, so there is no way to know whose coins they are. A בעל הבית grew the produce himself, so the coins can be traced back to him. In that case the buyer must return them.

keyTerms.meaning: A merchant who buys from many different sources
A private owner, here a farmer selling his own produce
He is obligated to return it

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence begins in the middle. The words 'they taught this only' come at the end of the previous עמוד, so this line is finishing a limitation that is already under way.

phrases.english: [This was taught only] in the case of one who buys from a merchant,
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence from the previous עמוד, about someone who finds coins inside produce he bought.

phrases.english: but in the case of one who buys from a private owner,
he is obligated to return [the coins].

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּלוֹקֵחַ מִן הַתַּגָּר, אֲבָל בְּלוֹקֵחַ מִבַּעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a limitation of the previous משנה that began on the prior עמוד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Found coins belong to the buyer only if he bought from a merchant. A buyer from a private owner must return them.

steps.title: A ברייתא says the same thing
steps.stepSummary: A תנא recites a ברייתא before רב נחמן that makes the same distinction between a merchant and a private owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so too, a תנא taught before רב נחמן: They taught this only about one who buys from a merchant. But one who buys from a private owner must return the coins.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support from a ברייתא that states exactly the same limitation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The limitation from Step 1 is now backed by an older source. This also sets up the next move, because רב נחמן is about to question that ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, a person whose job was to memorize and recite ברייתות in the study hall
And so too it was taught
They taught this only in the case of

phrases.english: And likewise the tanna taught
phrases.notes: This תנא is a reciter, someone who memorized teachings for the study hall, not one of the sages of the משנה.

phrases.english: before Rav Nachman:
They taught this only
in the case of one who buys from a merchant,
but in the case of one who buys from a private owner,
he is obligated to return [them].

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן תָּנֵי תַּנָּא קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports Step 1 with a ברייתא that says the same thing.
steps.raayaObject: The distinction between buying from a merchant and buying from a private owner.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא recited by the תנא before רב נחמן.

steps.title: Does the owner thresh by himself?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן objects that a private owner does not thresh his own grain, so the coins could belong to one of his workers.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to him: But does the owner thresh the grain himself?
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן challenges the ברייתא the תנא just recited.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole reason for returning the coins was that they could be traced to one person, the owner. But workers usually do the threshing. That means the coins might have come from a worker, and the owner would no longer be the clear owner of them.

keyTerms.meaning: But is it really so that...? (a word that opens a challenge)
Threshes it
By himself

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said to him:
But does the owner thresh it himself?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning of the ברייתא in Step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a buyer from a private owner must return the coins.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Workers thresh the grain, so the coins cannot be clearly linked to the owner.

steps.title: Should I erase the ברייתא?
steps.stepSummary: The תנא asks whether, because of this difficulty, he should remove the ברייתא from what he recites.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Should I erase it?
steps.whatsHappening: The תנא asks a practical question: since the ברייתא seems wrong, should he stop teaching it? This sets up רב נחמן's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question shows how serious רב נחמן's objection is. It raises the option of throwing the source out completely.

keyTerms.meaning: Should I erase it?
To erase or remove

phrases.english: He said to him: Should I erase it?
phrases.notes: Here the תנא is speaking, asking whether to drop this ברייתא from what he teaches.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the objection in Step 3 by asking whether to remove the source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the ברייתא should be removed because of רב נחמן's difficulty.

steps.title: Threshed by his כנעני slaves
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says not to erase it. Instead, read the ברייתא as a case where the owner's כנעני slave and maidservant did the threshing.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: No. Explain the teaching as a case where he threshed through his כנעני slave and maidservant.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן saves the ברייתא by limiting it to a specific case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner's own כנעני slaves did the threshing, the problem of outside workers disappears. Whatever the slaves have belongs to their master, so the coins can still be traced to the owner. The ruling of the ברייתא therefore stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Explain it as, interpret it as
Our teaching (here it means the ברייתא just recited)
A non-Jewish slave owned by a Jew
Maidservant

steps.whatToRemember: A buyer from a merchant keeps found coins. A buyer from a private owner returns them, in the case where the owner's own כנעני slaves threshed the grain.

phrases.english: He said to him: No,
interpret the teaching
phrases.notes: Here מתניתין means the ברייתא the תנא just said, not our משנה.

phrases.english: as a case where he threshed it through
his Canaanite slave and maidservant.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection in Step 3 and the question in Step 4.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to describe an ordinary owner whose hired workers thresh, which made it look wrong.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is talking about an owner whose כנעני slaves threshed, so the coins are his.

steps.title: The garment as the model for announcing
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה says the Torah singled out the שמלה to teach that any item with סימנים and with owners who would claim it must be announced.
steps.simpleTranslation: The garment too was included in 'all of these'. So why was it mentioned separately? To compare other things to it and teach you: just as a garment is special in that it has identifying marks and it has claimants, so too any item that has identifying marks and has claimants must be announced.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It explains why the פסוק names the שמלה separately when it was already included in the general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The garment was already covered by the general phrase, so naming it separately must teach something. It is a הקש: the garment becomes the model case. Its two features, סימנים and people who would claim it, become the test for which found items require הכרזה.

keyTerms.meaning: Garment
And why was it singled out?
To compare one thing to another and learn from it (הקש)
Identifying marks
Claimants, people who would come to claim it
To announce the find publicly

steps.whyThisMatters: These two features, סימנים and claimants, become the basic test for when a finder must announce what he found.

phrases.english: Mishnah:
The garment too was
included in 'all of these,'
and why was it singled out?
To compare [other items] to it,
to tell you:
Just as a garment is special
in that it has identifying marks
and it has claimants,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כׇּל דָּבָר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ סִימָנִין
phrases.english: so too any item that has identifying marks
and has claimants
[the finder] is obligated to announce it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף הַשִּׂמְלָה הָיְתָה בִּכְלַל כׇּל אֵלּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה and a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any found item that has סימנים and claimants must be announced, learned from the שמלה.

steps.title: Which general phrase?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the משנה means by 'included in all of these.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What is meant by 'included in all of these'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which general phrase in the פסוק the garment belonged to. This sets up רבא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words of the משנה are vague. The הקש only works once we know which general phrase originally included the garment.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion of the משנה
What is it?
Included in a general phrase

phrases.english: Gemara:
What is meant by 'included in all of these'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for clarification of a phrase in the משנה in Step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which general phrase in the פסוק included the garment.

steps.title: רבא: 'every lost item of your brother'
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the garment was included in the general phrase 'כל אבדת אחיך.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It was included in 'every lost item of your brother.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא names the general phrase in the פסוק that already covered the garment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק ends with 'כל אבדת אחיך,' which covers every lost object. Since that would already include a garment, naming the שמלה separately must be there to teach the הקש.

keyTerms.meaning: Your brother's lost item
Every, all

steps.whatToRemember: The שמלה was already covered by 'כל אבדת אחיך.' It was mentioned separately to teach that items with סימנים and claimants must be announced.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Included in 'every lost item of your brother.'
phrases.notes: דברים 22:3

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: בִּכְלַל כׇּל אֲבֵדַת אָחִיךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The general phrase is 'כל אבדת אחיך' in the פסוק.

steps.title: Why does the Torah list four lost items?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks why the Torah needs to name an ox, a donkey, a sheep and a garment, when one example might seem enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Why does the Torah need to write "ox," "donkey," "sheep" and "garment"?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא opens a new question about the פסוקים of returning lost items. This sets up the next steps, where he tries to find a lesson in each word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah usually does not waste words. If the rule is simply to return lost things, naming four different items looks extra. רבא wants to know what each one adds.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need it? (asking what a word adds)
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah
Garment

phrases.english: Rava said:
Why do I need that the Merciful One wrote
"ox," "donkey," "sheep," and "garment"?
phrases.notes: דברים 22:1–3

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: לְמָה לִי דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the garment was shown to be part of the general rule, רבא asks why all four specific items are named.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What each of the four named items teaches.

steps.title: The donkey teaches that saddle signs are enough
steps.stepSummary: All the items are needed. From שמלה alone we would think identifying signs must be on the item itself. חמור teaches that a donkey is returned even through signs on its saddle.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are necessary. If the Torah had written only "garment," I would say this applies only with witnesses or signs about the item itself. But for a donkey, where the witnesses or signs are about the saddle, I might say we don't return it. So the Torah wrote "donkey": even a donkey is returned through signs on the saddle.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers that the words are needed. He explains what the word חמור adds beyond שמלה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a garment, the signs are on the garment itself. With a donkey, the owner might know only signs on the saddle, which is a separate object. The word חמור teaches that such signs still count and the donkey goes back.

keyTerms.meaning: They are needed (each word teaches something)
I would have thought (a mistaken first idea)
Identifying signs
Saddle
We return (it)

phrases.english: They are necessary,
for if the Merciful One had written only garment,
I would have said:
this applies with witnesses about the item itself
or identifying signs on the item itself.
But a donkey, with witnesses about the saddle
or identifying signs on the saddle,
I might say we do not return it to him,
so the Merciful One wrote "donkey"
to teach that even a donkey is returned through signs on the saddle.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9 for the word חמור.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: חמור teaches that a donkey is returned even when the witnesses or signs relate only to its saddle.

steps.title: Why are ox and sheep written?
steps.stepSummary: רבא now asks what the words שור and שה add.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Ox" and "sheep," which the Torah wrote, why do I need them?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that חמור is explained, רבא asks about the other two animals. This sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The donkey and the garment have each been accounted for. The ox and the sheep still look extra, so רבא needs a lesson for each of them.

keyTerms.meaning: Ox
Sheep or lamb

phrases.english: "Ox" and "sheep,"
which the Merciful One wrote, why do I need them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבא's question, moving on to the remaining two items.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the words שור and שה teach.

steps.title: Ox and sheep teach returning sheared wool
steps.stepSummary: שור teaches that even the wool sheared from its tail must be returned, and שה teaches that the wool sheared from a sheep must be returned.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Ox" teaches that even the shearings of its tail must be returned, and "sheep" teaches that its shearings must be returned.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא suggests a lesson for each animal. Both are about returning wool that was sheared off.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that the duty to return covers not only the animal but also wool cut from it. The ox teaches this even for the small amount of hair from its tail. The sheep teaches it for its regular wool.

keyTerms.meaning: Shearing, wool that was cut off
Its tail

phrases.english: "Ox": to include even the shearings of its tail,
and "sheep": to include its shearings.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שור includes even tail-shearings, and שה includes the sheep's shearings.

steps.title: Ox alone would teach the sheep's wool too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that if even tail-hair from an ox must be returned, then sheep's wool, which is worth more, must surely be returned, so שה is still extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let the Torah write only "ox," teaching that even its tail-shearings must be returned, and all the more so a sheep's shearings!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer about שה. It argues that שה teaches nothing that שור doesn't already teach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tail-hair of an ox is minor. If the Torah requires returning even that, then sheep's wool, which is far more important, follows with a קל וחומר. So the word שה still has no job of its own.

keyTerms.meaning: Then let it write (only)
All the more so

phrases.english: But let the Merciful One write only "ox,"
teaching that even the shearings of its tail must be returned,
and all the more so "sheep" for its shearings!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the explanation of שה given in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that שה teaches the duty to return sheep's shearings.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר from the ox's tail-hair already covers sheep's wool, so the word שה is still unneeded.

steps.title: Two extra words remain unexplained
steps.stepSummary: רבא concedes that חמור in the pit verse, according to רבי יהודה, and שה in the lost-item verses, according to everyone, have no explanation.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: "Donkey" in the case of the pit, according to רבי יהודה, and "sheep" in the case of a lost item, according to everyone, are difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא drops his answer about שה and admits he cannot explain why it is written. He adds a second word in a different topic that is also unexplained.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of forcing an answer, רבא openly leaves the question standing. The word שה in the lost-item verses is a difficulty on every opinion. The word חמור in the pit verse is a difficulty only according to רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (dropping the earlier answer)
Pit, a category of damages
According to everyone
It is difficult (left unresolved)

steps.whatToRemember: חמור teaches that a donkey is returned through signs on its saddle. The word שה in the lost-item verses has no explanation and stays a קשיא.
steps.confusionAlert: קשיא here does not mean the rule is wrong. It only means that we don't know why the word שה was written.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
"Donkey" in the case of the pit, according to Rabbi Yehuda,
phrases.notes: שמות 21:33

phrases.english: and "sheep" in the case of a lost item,
according to everyone, are difficult.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the objection of step 13 and closes the discussion with an unresolved difficulty.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The word שה in the lost-item verses (on every opinion) and חמור in the pit verse (according to רבי יהודה) remain unexplained.

steps.title: Maybe the word 'sheep' teaches about returning dung
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא's admission that שה has no explanation. It suggests that שה teaches that a sheep's dung must be returned.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe the word 'sheep' comes to teach that we must return its dung?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is not ready to accept that the word שה is unexplained. It suggests a possible purpose: returning the animal's dung.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 14, רבא admitted that שה in the lost-item פסוקים teaches nothing new. Here the גמרא tries to rescue the word with a new idea. If dung must be returned, that would be a new חידוש not covered by the other items in the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: And say / but maybe; a way of suggesting another possibility
Animal dung
That it comes [to teach]

phrases.english: But say it comes for dung?
phrases.notes: 'It' is the word שה, the one רבא said had no explanation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's concession by offering a new purpose for שה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's admission that שה in the lost-item פסוקים has no explanation
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If dung must be returned, then שה has a real purpose, and רבא's admission is not needed.

steps.title: Dung is ownerless, so it is not a lost item
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the dung idea. Owners give up ownership of their animals' dung, so there is nothing to return.
steps.simpleTranslation: Dung: the owner gives up ownership of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the suggestion from Step 15. Dung does not need to be returned at all, so שה cannot be teaching that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person only has to return something that still belongs to someone. Owners normally declare their animals' dung הפקר, so it belongs to no one and is not an אבידה. That means the dung idea fails, and שה is still without a purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: He fully renounces ownership
Ownerless property that anyone may take

phrases.english: Dung — he renounces ownership of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the dung suggestion and keeps רבא's admission in place.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual distinction: the item is ownerless
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שה might teach that dung must be returned.
steps.terutzMaskana: Dung is הפקר, so there is no duty to return it, and שה cannot be teaching that.

steps.title: Maybe 'sheep' teaches that סימנין work by Torah law
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries again. Maybe שה teaches that we return an item based on סימנין, which would settle the open question of whether סימנין are דאורייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or perhaps it comes to teach about identifying marks, since we asked: are identifying marks a Torah law or a rabbinic law? The Torah wrote 'sheep' to teach that we return items even based on identifying marks, so identifying marks are a Torah law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second purpose for שה: it teaches that סימנין are accepted by Torah law. If that were true, it would also prove one side of a famous open question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is an open question (איבעיא) whether returning an item based on סימנין is דאורייתא or דרבנן. If the Torah needed to write שה to teach that סימנין work, then סימנין would be a Torah rule. This step does two things at once: it gives שה a purpose, and it tries to prove that סימנין are דאורייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: Identifying marks the owner describes to prove the item is his
We asked / it was an open question for us
By Torah law
By rabbinic law
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

phrases.english: And perhaps it comes for identifying marks,
as we raised a question:
phrases.notes: The גמרא raises this very question on its own a little later, in step 36.

phrases.english: Are identifying marks from the Torah or from the Rabbis?
The Merciful One wrote 'sheep,'
to teach that we return even based on identifying marks,
and identifying marks are from the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the dung idea failed, proposes a different purpose for שה.
steps.raayaObject: That סימנין are דאורייתא, and that שה has a purpose
steps.raayaSupportSource: The extra word שה in the lost-item פסוקים

steps.title: The משנה already learns סימנין from 'garment'
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected. The תנא of the משנה learns the rule of סימנין from שמלה, so שה is not the source for סימנין.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answered: since the תנא teaches identifying marks in connection with 'garment', as it says, 'What is special about a garment? It has identifying marks and it has people who claim it, so one must announce it. So too, anything that has identifying marks and people who claim it must be announced.' Conclude from this that 'sheep' does not come to teach about identifying marks.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the idea from Step 17. The משנה already ties סימנין to the word שמלה, so the word שה is not needed for that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה derives from שמלה that any item with סימנין and with owners who would claim it must be announced. Since the source for סימנין is שמלה, the word שה cannot be the source. So שה stays without an explanation, and the question of סימנין דאורייתא is not settled here.

keyTerms.meaning: Garment, one of the items in the פסוק
Claimants, owners who would come looking for the item
To publicly announce a found item
Learn from this / conclude from it

steps.whatToRemember: Both attempts to explain שה fail. Dung is הפקר, and סימנין are already learned from שמלה. So רבא's admission in Step 14 still stands.

phrases.english: They said: since the תנא teaches them,
identifying marks together with 'garment,'
as it teaches: what is special about a garment?
phrases.notes: This is quoted from our משנה.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ סִימָנִין וְיֵשׁ לָהּ תּוֹבְעִין –
phrases.english: That it has identifying marks and it has claimants —
one is obligated to announce it,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כׇּל דָּבָר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ סִימָנִין
phrases.english: so too, anything that has identifying marks
and has claimants — one is obligated to announce it.
Conclude from this that 'sheep'
does not come for identifying marks.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי מִדְּקָתָנֵי לְהוּ תַּנָּא לְסִימָנִין גַּבֵּי שִׂמְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proposal that שה teaches סימנין.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole idea that שה is the source for סימנין, so the proof that סימנין are דאורייתא also falls.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה already learns סימנין from שמלה, so שה is not needed for it.

steps.title: An item worth less than a פרוטה is not an אבידה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a lost item worth less than a שוה פרוטה does not need to be returned. The תנא קמא learns it from 'אשר תאבד' and רבי יהודה learns it from 'ומצאתה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'which shall be lost' excludes a lost item that is not worth a פרוטה. רבי יהודה says: 'and you have found it' excludes a lost item that is not worth a פרוטה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a ברייתא. It sets a minimum value, a שוה פרוטה, for the מצוה of returning a lost item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions agree that an item worth less than a פרוטה is not covered by the מצוה. They only quote different words from the same פסוק as the source. This sets up the obvious question in the next step: what is the difference between them?

keyTerms.meaning: To exclude
A lost item
Worth a פרוטה, the smallest coin that counts as real value

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: 'which shall be lost' —
phrases.notes: דברים 22:3

phrases.aramaic: פְּרָט לַאֲבֵידָה שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ שָׁוֶה פְּרוּטָה.
phrases.english: excludes a lost item that is not worth a פרוטה.
רבי יהודה says: 'and you have found it' —
phrases.notes: The next words in the same פסוק.

phrases.aramaic: פְּרָט לַאֲבֵידָה שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ שָׁוֶה פְּרוּטָה.
phrases.english: excludes a lost item that is not worth a פרוטה.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן אֲשֶׁר תֹּאבַד פְּרָט לַאֲבֵידָה שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ שָׁוֶה פְּרוּטָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new topic after the discussion of שה ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lost item worth less than a שוה פרוטה does not have to be returned. The two opinions learn this from different words in the פסוק.

steps.title: What is the difference between the two opinions?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between the תנא קמא and רבי יהודה, since they seem to say the same law.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why two opinions are listed when both reach the same law. This question sets up אביי's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides exclude an item worth less than a פרוטה. The גמרא wants to know whether they disagree on any real case, or only on something else.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?

phrases.english: What is between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the disagreement in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the תנא קמא and רבי יהודה disagree on any practical law

steps.title: They only disagree about which words of the פסוק teach the rule
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that there is no practical difference. They only argue over which words of the פסוק are the source.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: the difference between them is only how the פסוק is read. One Sage learns it from 'which shall be lost', and the other Sage learns it from 'and you have found it'.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question. The two opinions agree on the law, and they only disagree about where in the פסוק the law comes from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sometimes a מחלוקת is not about the law at all but about the source. Here both sides agree that less than a פרוטה is not an אבידה. The only difference is which words in the פסוק each one uses to teach it.

keyTerms.meaning: The way the פסוק is read and explained
One Sage (literally 'master')
He learns it from

steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי, both sides agree that an item worth less than a שוה פרוטה is not an אבידה. Their מחלוקת is only about which words in the פסוק teach this. רבא disagrees in step 31 and finds a practical difference.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: מַשְׁמָעוּת דּוֹרְשִׁין אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ.
phrases.english: אביי said: the meaning they read into the verse is what is between them.
One Sage learns it from 'which shall be lost,'
and the other Sage learns it from 'and you have found it.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי מַשְׁמָעוּת דּוֹרְשִׁין אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: There is no practical difference. They only disagree about which words of the פסוק are the source.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to אביי, both agree that an item worth less than a פרוטה need not be returned, and they differ only in the source.

steps.title: What does the תנא קמא learn from 'ומצאתה'?
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא learns the שוה פרוטה rule from 'אשר תאבד', so the גמרא asks what he does with the word 'ומצאתה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who learns it from 'which shall be lost', what does he do with 'and you have found it'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the תנא קמא a question. Since he uses 'אשר תאבד' for the שוה פרוטה rule, what does he learn from the word 'ומצאתה'?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes that every word in a פסוק teaches something. רבי יהודה uses 'ומצאתה' for the שוה פרוטה rule, so the תנא קמא must have some other use for it. The גמרא wants to know what that use is.

keyTerms.meaning: And according to the one who learns it from
What does he do with it? (what does he learn from this word?)
'And you have found it', a word from the פסוק

phrases.english: And according to the one who learns it from 'which shall be lost'
phrases.notes: This is the תנא קמא, who learned the שוה פרוטה rule from these words in step 19.

phrases.english: what does he do with this 'and you have found it'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from אביי's answer that the two opinions only argue about the source. Now the גמרא checks what each side does with the other side's word.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the תנא קמא learns from the word 'ומצאתה', since he does not use it for the שוה פרוטה rule.

steps.title: The תנא קמא uses 'ומצאתה' for רבנאי's teaching
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא needs 'ומצאתה' for רבנאי's rule that an item counts as 'found' once it comes into the finder's hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: He needs that word for רבנאי's teaching. רבנאי said: 'and you have found it' means that it came into his hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the תנא קמא uses 'ומצאתה' for a different lesson, the teaching of רבנאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבנאי reads 'ומצאתה' as defining what 'finding' means. It means the item actually came into the finder's hand. So the word is not extra for the תנא קמא. It has its own job.

keyTerms.meaning: He needs it (for another teaching)
That it came into his hand
It means / it implies

phrases.english: He needs that for the teaching of Rabbenai,
as Rabbenai said:
'and you have found it' means that it came into his hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The תנא קמא uses 'ומצאתה' for רבנאי's teaching that 'finding' means the item came into the finder's hand.

steps.title: What does רבי יהודה learn from 'אשר תאבד'?
steps.stepSummary: Now the גמרא asks the same question in the other direction. רבי יהודה uses 'ומצאתה', so what does he do with 'אשר תאבד'?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to the one who learns it from 'and you have found it', what does he do with 'which shall be lost'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to רבי יהודה and asks the same question. Since he uses 'ומצאתה' for the שוה פרוטה rule, what does he learn from 'אשר תאבד'?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the mirror image of step 22. The תנא קמא's source words, 'אשר תאבד', still need some job in רבי יהודה's view.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Which shall be lost', words from the פסוק

phrases.english: And according to the one who learns it from 'and you have found it',
phrases.notes: This is רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: what does he do with this 'which shall be lost'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel question to step 22, now asked from רבי יהודה's side.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What רבי יהודה learns from the words 'אשר תאבד', since he does not use them for the שוה פרוטה rule.

steps.title: רבי יהודה uses 'אשר תאבד' for the item swept away by a river
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה needs 'אשר תאבד' for רבי יוחנן's teaching: you only have to return an item that is lost to the owner but can still be found by people. An item swept away by a river is lost to everyone, so the finder may keep it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He needs it for רבי יוחנן's teaching. רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחאי: From where do we know that a lost item swept away by a river is permitted? Because the פסוק says, 'so shall you do with every lost item of your brother, which shall be lost from him and you have found it.' This means an item that is lost to him but can be found by any person. That leaves out an item that is lost to him and cannot be found by any person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יהודה uses 'אשר תאבד' for רבי יוחנן's rule that an item swept away by a river may be kept by the finder.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'אשר תאבד ממנו' (lost from him) say the item is lost only to the owner. They imply that other people could still find it. An item swept away by a river is lost to everyone, so the מצוה to return it does not apply and the finder may keep it.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know?
That a river swept away
Permitted (the finder may keep it)
Can be found by any person
Is left out (from the rule)

steps.whatToRemember: Each opinion still uses both words of the פסוק. The תנא קמא uses 'ומצאתה' for רבנאי: 'finding' means it came into your hand. רבי יהודה uses 'אשר תאבד' for רבי יוחנן: an item lost to everyone, like one swept away by a river, may be kept.
steps.whyThisMatters: רבי יוחנן's rule is an important exception within the laws of returning lost items. It is still a lost item, but the מצוה to return it does not apply when it is lost to the whole world.

phrases.english: He needs it for the teaching of Rabbi Yoḥanan.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי:
phrases.english: As Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai:
From where do we know that a lost item that a river swept away
is permitted?
phrases.notes: He means the finder is allowed to keep it.

phrases.english: As it says: 'So shall you do with every lost item of your brother,'
phrases.notes: דברים 22:3

phrases.english: 'which shall be lost from him, and you have found it'
meaning an item that is lost from him
but can be found by any person,
which leaves out this one, which is lost from him
and cannot be found by any person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24, so both opinions are shown to use every word of the פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יהודה uses 'אשר תאבד' for רבי יוחנן's rule (from רבי שמעון בן יוחאי) that an item lost to everyone, like one swept away by a river, may be kept.

steps.title: Where does רבי יהודה learn רבנאי's rule?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה already uses 'ומצאתה' for the פרוטה rule, so the גמרא asks where he gets רבנאי's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one (רבי יהודה), where does he get רבנאי's rule from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to רבי יהודה. He already used 'ומצאתה' for the פרוטה rule, so where does he get רבנאי's teaching that an item counts as found once it comes into your hand?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 23 the תנא קמא learned רבנאי's rule from 'ומצאתה'. רבי יהודה already used that word for the פרוטה rule. So the גמרא wants to know his source for רבנאי's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one (the other opinion)
From where does he learn it?

phrases.english: And the other one,
phrases.notes: This means רבי יהודה, who learned the פרוטה rule from 'ומצאתה'.

phrases.english: this rule of רבנאי, from where does he get it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors step 24. Now the question is asked about רבי יהודה and רבנאי's rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: רבי יהודה's source for רבנאי's rule

steps.title: רבי יהודה learns it from 'ומצאתה' too
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה also learns רבנאי's rule from 'ומצאתה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns it from 'And you have found it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יהודה learns רבנאי's rule from 'ומצאתה' as well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same word teaches him two things: the פרוטה rule and רבנאי's rule. The extra letter ו ('and') at the start of 'ומצאתה' gives him the second lesson.

keyTerms.meaning: He derives it (literally, 'it comes out for him')
'And you have found it' (דברים 22:3)

phrases.english: He derives it from 'and you have found it.'
phrases.notes: He already uses this word for the פרוטה rule, so he gets one more lesson from the extra 'ו', meaning 'and'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יהודה derives רבנאי's rule from 'ומצאתה' as well.

steps.title: Where does the תנא קמא learn רבי יוחנן's rule?
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא already uses 'אשר תאבד' for the פרוטה rule, so the גמרא asks where he gets רבי יוחנן's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one (the תנא קמא), where does he get רבי יוחנן's rule from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks about the תנא קמא. He used 'אשר תאבד' for the פרוטה rule, so where does he get רבי יוחנן's rule about an item swept away by a river?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 25 רבי יהודה learned רבי יוחנן's rule from 'אשר תאבד'. The תנא קמא already used those words for the פרוטה rule, so he needs a different source.

phrases.english: And the other one,
phrases.notes: Now it means the תנא קמא, who learned the פרוטה rule from 'אשר תאבד'.

phrases.english: this rule of רבי יוחנן, from where does he get it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ, הָא דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מְנָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The same question in the other direction, now aimed at the תנא קמא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The תנא קמא's source for רבי יוחנן's rule

steps.title: The תנא קמא learns it from 'ממנו'
steps.stepSummary: The תנא קמא learns רבי יוחנן's rule from the word 'ממנו', meaning 'from him'.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns it from 'from him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the תנא קמא learns רבי יוחנן's rule from the word 'ממנו' in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'אשר תאבד ממנו', meaning 'which is lost from him'. The words 'from him' show the item is lost only to the owner, not to everyone. An item swept away by a river is lost to everyone, so it does not need to be returned.

keyTerms.meaning: 'From him'. The item is lost to the owner, but not to everyone.

phrases.english: He derives it from 'from him.'
phrases.notes: The full phrase in the פסוק is 'אשר תאבד ממנו' (דברים 22:3).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The תנא קמא derives רבי יוחנן's rule from 'ממנו'.

steps.title: רבי יהודה does not learn from 'ממנו'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why רבי יהודה needed 'אשר תאבד': he does not learn anything from 'ממנו'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one? He does not learn anything from 'from him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא briefly asks why רבי יהודה doesn't also use 'ממנו', and answers that he does not learn anything from that word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains step 25. רבי יהודה does not learn anything from 'ממנו', so he had to use 'אשר תאבד' for רבי יוחנן's rule. Now each side's treatment of every word is accounted for, which completes אביי's approach that they argue only about the source.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not learn it from there (literally, 'it does not mean this to him')

steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי, both sides agree on the law. Each one just assigns the words 'אשר תאבד', 'ממנו' and 'ומצאתה' differently.

phrases.english: And the other one?
phrases.notes: Back to רבי יהודה: why doesn't he learn from 'ממנו' too?

phrases.english: He does not learn anything from 'from him.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the word-by-word check by explaining רבי יהודה's view of 'ממנו'.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יהודה does not learn anything from 'ממנו', so he needs 'אשר תאבד' for רבי יוחנן's rule.

steps.title: רבא: they differ about a פרוטה that dropped in value
steps.stepSummary: רבא disagrees with אביי. He says the two views differ about an item worth a פרוטה when lost that is worth less than a פרוטה when found.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The difference between them is a פרוטה that dropped in value. The one who learns from 'which is lost' says you must return it. The one who learns from 'and you have found it' says you need not.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different approach from אביי. He says there is a practical difference, in the case of an item whose value dropped below a פרוטה between when it was lost and when it was found.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the rule comes from 'אשר תאבד', the value at the time of losing counts. It was worth a פרוטה then, so you must return it. If the rule comes from 'ומצאתה', the value at the time of finding counts. It is worth less than a פרוטה then, so you need not return it.

keyTerms.meaning: An item worth a פרוטה that dropped in value
There is a difference between them
There is not (here: there is no duty to return it)

steps.confusionAlert: 'איכא' and 'ליכא' here mean 'there is a duty to return' and 'there is no duty to return'. They do not mean the item exists or doesn't exist.
steps.whyThisMatters: This turns what looked like an argument only about the source into a real difference in the law.

phrases.english: רבא said:
A פרוטה that dropped in value is the difference between them,
the one who says it comes from 'which is lost': there is a duty to return,
and the one who says it comes from 'and you have found it': there is not.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: פְּרוּטָה שֶׁהוּזְלָה אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with אביי's claim in step 21 that there is no practical difference.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the 'אשר תאבד' view you must return a פרוטה that dropped in value. According to the 'ומצאתה' view you need not.

steps.title: Challenge: 'ומצאתה' still requires value when found
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא. Even the 'אשר תאבד' view needs the word 'ומצאתה', and at finding the item is not worth a פרוטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But even for the one who learns from 'which is lost', we still need 'and you have found it', and here that is missing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבא's difference. Even the 'אשר תאבד' view should require the item to be worth a פרוטה when found, so he too should say you need not return it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק has both phrases. So even if 'אשר תאבד' is the main source, 'ומצאתה' should still require a valuable find. If so, both views agree there is no duty to return, and רבא's difference disappears. The answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: We require
And according to the one who says

phrases.english: But according to the one who says 'which is lost':
don't we still require 'and you have found it'? And it is missing!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר ״אֲשֶׁר תֹּאבַד״ – הָא בָּעֵינַן ״וּמְצָאתָהּ״, וְלֵיכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's practical difference from step 31.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that the 'אשר תאבד' view requires returning a פרוטה that dropped in value
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק also says 'ומצאתה', so even this view should require the item to be worth a פרוטה when found. Here it is not, so he too should say there is no duty to return it.

steps.title: A new case: the item went up in value
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a new difference. Take an item worth less than a פרוטה when lost but worth a פרוטה when found. The 'ומצאתה' view says you must return it; the 'אשר תאבד' view says you do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the difference between them is a פרוטה that went up in value. The one who learns from 'and you have found it' says you must return it. The one who learns from 'which shall be lost' says you don't have to.
steps.whatsHappening: The last case was knocked down, so the גמרא flips it around. Now the item was worth too little when lost but enough when found.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each view looks at a different moment. 'ומצאתה' (and you have found it) looks at the moment of finding, and then the item is worth a פרוטה, so you must return it. 'אשר תאבד' (which shall be lost) looks at the moment of losing, and then it was worth less than a פרוטה, so there is no duty to return it.

keyTerms.meaning: It became more expensive (went up in value)
There is a difference between them (the practical case where they disagree)
There is not (no obligation)
'And you have found it', a word from the פסוק about returning lost items

phrases.english: Rather,
a פרוטה that went up in value is the difference between them.
The one who says 'and you have found it': there is a duty to return it.
And the one who says 'which shall be lost': there is no duty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the case that Step 32 knocked down with the opposite case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The views differ when an item lost its value between losing and finding (Step 31).
steps.terutzMaskana: Maybe they differ when the item gained value between losing and finding.

steps.title: The 'ומצאתה' view still needs the item to be worth something when lost
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the new case. The 'ומצאתה' view also needs the words 'אשר תאבד', and when this item was lost it was not worth a פרוטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But even for the one who learns from 'and you have found it', don't we still need 'which shall be lost'? And here it isn't there!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the new case, the same way Step 32 attacked the last one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both phrases are in the same פסוק, so both views accept both of them. Even the 'ומצאתה' view must agree that the item has to be worth a פרוטה when lost. In this case it was not, so both views would say there is no duty to return it, and there is no disagreement left.

don't we still need 'which shall be lost'?

phrases.english: And it isn't there!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר ״וּמְצָאתָהּ״, הָא בָּעֵינַן ״אֲשֶׁר תֹּאבַד״ וְלֵיכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the case proposed in Step 33.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the 'ומצאתה' view requires returning an item that rose to a פרוטה only after it was lost.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both views must accept the whole פסוק. 'אשר תאבד' requires value at the time of loss, so the 'ומצאתה' view would also exempt this item.

steps.title: The real difference: the item went up, down, and up again
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא's final case: an item worth a פרוטה when lost dropped below a פרוטה in between, then rose again by the time it was found. The 'אשר תאבד' view says you must return it. The 'ומצאתה' view says the item must be worth a פרוטה the whole time, from loss until finding.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the difference between them is a פרוטה that went up, then went down, then went back up again. The one who learns from 'which shall be lost' says you must return it. The one who learns from 'and you have found it' says the item needs the value of a lost item from the time it was lost until the time it was found.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a case that survives both challenges. The item is worth a פרוטה at both ends but not in the middle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now both views agree the item was worth a פרוטה when lost and when found. The 'אשר תאבד' view checks only those two moments, so you must return it. The 'ומצאתה' view demands the value the whole time without a break, so the drop in the middle frees the finder from returning it.

keyTerms.meaning: It became cheaper (went down in value)
And it went back (again)
The minimum value of a found item (a פרוטה)
From the time of losing until the time of finding

steps.whatToRemember: Final answer: both views need a פרוטה at loss and at finding. The 'ומצאתה' view also needs it the whole time in between.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the sides here. In this case the 'אשר תאבד' view is the one that says you must return it, and the 'ומצאתה' view is the stricter test that frees the finder.

from the time it was lost until the time it was found.

steps.title: Are identifying marks from the Torah or from the Rabbis?
steps.stepSummary: A new topic opens. The חכמים ask whether returning a lost item based on סימנים (identifying marks) is a Torah law or a rabbinic law.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked to them: are identifying marks a Torah law or a rabbinic law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a brand-new question. It asks how strong the law of סימנים is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who describes a lost item's סימנים gets it back. The question is whether the Torah itself trusts סימנים (דאורייתא), or whether the Rabbis made this rule (דרבנן).

steps.title: What practical difference does it make?

steps.deeperAnalysis: Either way, we already return lost items based on סימנים. So the גמרא asks for a real case where the answer would change the outcome, and that case comes next.
